overview: tripline is a CI gate for detection rules. It compiles Sigma rules to Python, replays recorded telemetry for 14 ATT&CK techniques through them on every pull request, and fails the build when a rule that should fire stays quiet. Version 0.3.0 adds a benign corpus, a sweep of evasion variants and a coverage figure split by who wrote the passing rules.

The result that started it: Atomic Red Team's T1548.001 tests were recorded on a GitHub-hosted Linux runner, giving 36 events, 2 of them the attack itself (two chmod executions). SigmaHQ's stock Setuid and Setgid rule flagged 0 of the 2. The replacement rule in the repository flags both.

Across the 14 scenarios, 13 pass and 1 (Windows) is pending. Weighted coverage is 98%, but 52% on unmodified SigmaHQ rules alone, because the rest depends on rules written in the repository. In the evasion sweep, 200 of 251 hand-written variants were caught, with 2 false-positive matches on a 675-event benign corpus.
All evidence is recorded telemetry replayed offline, one recording per scenario. It is a recall check, not a measure of live detection.

sinkline.lede: Reads Python web code and flags places where request data reaches a dangerous call, such as a SQL query, without being cleaned first.

plain.what: It follows data from a web request through functions and files. It reports a finding only if the data reaches a dangerous call without the right clean-up for that kind of bug.
plain.why: Escaping HTML does nothing for a SQL query, so a tool has to know which clean-up fits which bug.
plain.found: On ten categories of OWASP BenchmarkPython (score = true-positive rate minus false-positive rate), 0.4.1 scored +0.21 and Bandit +0.07. Version 0.5.1 scores +0.52, but those fixes were chosen by reading 0.4.1's failures, so it is not a held-out score. Across all 14 categories Bandit still leads.

sinkline.blurb: A static taint analyzer for Python web apps. On a held-out set of 219 labeled bugs from CodeQL's Python tests it found 88, against 34 for Bandit and 53 for Semgrep, and missed 60%. Labels and scorer were frozen before the run.
sinkline.label: Held-out test, frozen before the run

og.line: held-out labeled bugs found. Bandit 34, Semgrep 53. It missed 60%, and found none in 127 bugs of classes it does not cover.

overview: sinkline is a static analyzer for Python web apps. It follows attacker-controlled input across functions and files and reports a finding only when the input reaches a dangerous call, such as a SQL query or a shell command, without a sanitizer for that bug class. It has 43 rules mapped to OWASP Top 10 and CWE, SARIF output and a GitHub Action, and it has no dependencies.

Held-out result: 346 labeled bugs from CodeQL's Python query tests, with labels, scorer and rules frozen before anything was run and no tuning afterwards. On the 219 bugs in classes sinkline has rules for, it found 88 (40%), with 77% of its findings real. Bandit found 34 (16%) at 77%, and Semgrep OSS with its registry rules found 53 (24%) at 46%. On the 127 bugs in classes it does not attempt, such as weak crypto and cookie flags, it found none and Bandit found 30.

Turning the interprocedural analysis off changed nothing on this set, so its snippets do not test it. The earlier figures are not held out: on OWASP BenchmarkPython's ten taint categories 0.4.1 scored +0.21 and 0.5.1 scores +0.52 (Bandit +0.07), but those fixes were chosen from the failures of 0.4.1, and over all 14 categories Bandit leads.
A separate sample report page shows sinkline's HTML output.

hero2.caption: The earlier benchmark: on OWASP BenchmarkPython, sinkline 0.5.0 found 175 of 240 real bugs against 31 for Bandit and 18 for Semgrep, and flagged more safe code. These fixes were chosen from the suite's misses, so it is not a held-out result.
hero2.label: benchmark chart

overview: kevgate is a small FastAPI service that takes vulnerability scanner findings and returns a remediation queue ranked by CISA KEV listing, EPSS, CVSS and asset criticality. The repository also shows what shipping a small service carefully looks like: hashed, scoped API keys, rate limits, a hardened container, a Helm chart, Terraform and a GitHub Actions security pipeline that tests those controls.

Real-data run: a scan of four old public container images produced 1,112 findings, 10 of them on CISA's list of flaws being exploited. A CVSS-only sort puts the first of those at about rank 40 on average, and the 10 average rank 246. kevgate puts all 10 in the top 10. That is partly by design, since KEV listing is an input to the score, and it is one run.
Engineering check: six defects survived the test suite under mutation testing. Tests added in v0.1.1 kill all six, and the suite grew from 227 to 277 tests (298 on main).
Scope: one replica, SQLite, and Terraform applied only to LocalStack. Nothing is deployed to a real AWS account.

overview: kevgate-admit is a Kubernetes validating admission webhook written in Go. When a workload is created it checks each container image against existing scan reports, using the same risk model as kevgate, and denies, warns or allows according to the namespace policy. It does not scan images itself.

Going back over the first version turned up five weaknesses: a malformed image reference was accepted, an option could drop a KEV finding, an outage was untested, scan evidence was unauthenticated and there was no published image. v0.1.0 closes all five, each with a test, a CI run or a recorded response. It adds strict image-reference parsing, optional signed scan reports and a signed image on GHCR. 93 tests, 95% coverage.

In the kind cluster test, five demo workloads gave three denials, one allowed workload and one admitted with a warning in audit mode. The outage test shows that failurePolicy Fail rejects new Pods while the webhook is down and Ignore lets through a Pod the policy would deny. The scan data is synthetic.
It does not verify image signatures at admission.

fuzzdiff.lede: A web-request parser rewritten from C into memory-safe Rust, checked by feeding both versions the same bytes and listing every difference.

plain.what: picohttpparser is an HTTP parser written in C. It was ported to safe Rust, then the C original, the port and a third parser (httparse) were run on the same input.
plain.why: A rewrite can change behavior without anyone noticing. Running the original next to the copy shows where.
plain.found: 5 bugs were planted to see whether the checks would notice. The 0.1.0 tests missed 2; 0.2.0 catches all 5. Against the C original there were 0 differences in 2,000,000 inputs. No vulnerability was found.

overview: fuzzdiff ports picohttpparser, an HTTP/1.x parser written in C, to safe Rust. The C original, the Rust port and a second parser (httparse) are then run on the same input, and every difference is reported. A rewrite can change behavior without anyone noticing; running the original next to the copy shows where.

To test the harness, 5 bugs were planted. The 0.1.0 tests missed 2 of them; v0.2.0 detects all 5, although one is caught only by a hand-built case because the random generator never builds that input. Against the C original there were 0 differences in 2,000,000 inputs. Against httparse, 609,278 inputs disagree, all in documented classes of leniency.

The fuzz runs are short smoke runs of two minutes per leg, and Miri covers the pure-Rust crate only. The Rust port is about 1.4x to 1.5x slower on head parsing, and the cause was not profiled. No vulnerability was found. This is sampling, not proof.

kev-risk-prioritization.lede: A short Python script that ranks scan findings so the known-exploited ones come first.

plain.what: It scores each finding from KEV listing, asset criticality, EPSS and CVSS, using weights chosen by hand, and sorts by that score. It is not an implementation of CISA BOD 26-04.
plain.why: Sorting by severity alone can bury the vulnerabilities attackers are already using.
plain.found: On 20 synthetic findings, a CVSS-only sort puts 9 of the 12 known-exploited ones in its top 12, and the risk score puts all 12 there. That shows how the formula orders findings, not that it speeds up fixing. The weights are not validated.

try.text: Move the four weights and watch the ranking reorder.

hero.alt: Left: EPSS scores of 1,779 known-exploited CVEs against 5,000 others, medians 0.533 and 0.006, AUC 0.9515. Right: this tool puts all 100 KEV findings of a 2,000-row list in its top 100, EPSS alone puts 65 and asset criticality alone puts 10. Bottom: the AUC is partly circular and the weights are unvalidated.
hero.caption: On the real KEV catalog and EPSS scores, EPSS separates known-exploited CVEs from the rest with an AUC of 0.9515, but that result is partly circular because EPSS is trained on exploitation data that overlaps with KEV, so it is not validation of either. The tool's 100 of 100 comes mostly from its weights.

kev-risk-prioritization.label: Synthetic findings, real KEV and EPSS snapshot

og.line: KEV findings in the top 12 on 20 synthetic findings: risk score vs CVSS-only sort. Weights not validated.

overview: kev-risk-prioritization is a standard-library Python script that scores each finding from CISA KEV listing, asset criticality, EPSS and CVSS, using weights chosen by hand (0.40, 0.25, 0.20, 0.20), and sorts by that score. It is not an implementation of CISA BOD 26-04. Sorting by severity alone can bury the vulnerabilities attackers are already using; this orders them first.

On 20 synthetic findings, a CVSS-only sort puts 9 of the 12 known-exploited ones in its top 12 and the risk score puts all 12 there. That shows how the formula orders findings, not that it speeds up fixing.

On a real KEV and EPSS snapshot, EPSS separates known-exploited CVEs from the rest with an AUC of 0.9515. That result is partly circular, because EPSS is trained on exploitation data that overlaps with KEV, so it validates neither signal. The weights are unvalidated. kevgate supersedes this tool for the real-data case. The script uses only the CVSS and EPSS values supplied to it.

vulnlab.label: Own code, loopback only

og.line: fixes verified by the lab's own tests. SSRF, SQL injection in ORDER BY, IDOR. Localhost only.

overview: vulnlab is a localhost-only lab of three small Flask services, each with one textbook web bug: SSRF through a redirect, SQL injection in ORDER BY, and a missing object-level permission check (IDOR). Each lab has a fixed version, tests that show the impact on the vulnerable service and then fail against the fix, and a Sigma rule replayed on recorded logs. 137 tests pass.

It also records where static analysis is wrong. sinkline reports 2 of the 3 bugs and also reports both fixed versions of those two, which are false positives. It reports nothing on the permission check, because that bug is not a taint flow. The detection rules alert on the attempts in all three labs and fire on the fixed services too, because they see attempts, not impact.

The bugs were written for the lab and are simpler than real ones. There are no CVEs and no findings against real software, and the services bind to loopback only. This is a training lab, not vulnerability research.

failed_first.text: The stock SigmaHQ Setuid and Setgid rule flagged 0 of the 2 attack events (the two chmod executions) among 36 recorded events. A replacement rule flags both.

Weighted coverage is 98% (61 of 62 points), but only 52% (32 of 62, 8 scenarios) passes on unmodified SigmaHQ rules alone. The other 5 passing scenarios (29 points) need a rule written in the tripline repository.
Against 251 generated command-line variants of three Linux attacks, the expected rules catch 200. The stock setuid rule catches 0 of 108 setuid variants; the replacement catches 106.
On a 675-event benign Linux corpus, SigmaHQ's New Cron File Created matched 2 events (a chkrootkit install). 20 of 26 rules, all Windows and AWS, were not evaluated.
1 of the 7 Windows scenarios (T1027) has no accepted recording and counts as zero in both the 98% and the 52%.

On the independent OWASP BenchmarkPython suite, 0.4.1 scored +0.21 on the 10 taint categories, with 0 of 16 LDAP and 5 of 51 XPath cases reported. 0.5.1 scores +0.52 (the same per-test table as 0.5.0), but the fixes were chosen from those failures, so it is not a held-out score.
Over all 14 categories Bandit leads (+0.36 against +0.27): sinkline has no check for weak hashes, weak random numbers, cookie flags or session contents.
The GitHub Action put its inputs into a shell line, a script-injection flaw in its own code. Fixed in 0.4.1.
Six deliberate defects survived 227 tests, including swapping the constant-time key comparison for ==. The code was correct, but no test would have failed. 0.1.1 adds tests that kill all six.
The image parser accepted ghcr.io/org/../evil, and ignoreUnfixed could let a KEV finding with no fix pass denyKev. Both are fixed in v0.1.0.

sinkline reports the fixed versions of the SSRF and SQL injection labs too, because it does not recognize a custom allow-list or address check as a sanitizer, and reports nothing on the IDOR lab, which is not a taint flow.

A second pass over 0.1.0 found that the fixed SSRF service answered 500 to malformed URLs, that both IDOR variants issued a login token for an unknown user with a null password, and that no test failed if the fixed SSRF service's address check was removed. All three are fixed in 0.1.1 and each has a test.
A mutation sweep found two one-line changes (a chunk-overhead ratio and a status-line guard) that none of the 0.1.0 tests noticed. 0.2.0 names them as seeded bugs and adds cases that catch them.
The harness treated any folded-header error in strict mode as the documented deviation, which would have hidden a real bug. The exception is now narrowed.

Earlier text called the score "in the spirit of" CISA BOD 26-04, and a measurements table reported properties of invented values. Both were corrected: it is a weighted score of its own design, and the table was removed.

In 0.2.0 a finding without CVSS was scored on a different scale from one with it (the same KEV finding scored 73.5 without CVSS and 59.5 with CVSS 0.0), so a mixed list was ranked with incomparable scores. 0.3.0 refuses such a list unless --allow-mixed, which scores every row without CVSS.
